title: Dairy farm records and administrative processes

lessons.title: The dairy office: herd and production records
lessons.html:
Admin is part of farming

In this work experience module you will keep real records and carry out admin tasks on a dairy, supervised by the farm manager or office staff. Your logbook should show which records you kept and how you used them.

Herd records

  • Animal register: every animal's ID, date of birth, dam, sire, and movements in and out.
  • Calving and breeding: heats, services, pregnancy checks, calvings, dry-off dates.
  • Health and treatment: diagnosis, medicine, dose, who treated, withdrawal dates.
  • Milk recording: individual yields and test results from the milk recording scheme, if the farm takes part.

Production records

  • Daily litres and bulk tank temperatures.
  • Milk collection slips and the buyer's monthly statement with quality results.
  • Feed received, used and in stock.
  • Pasture records: camp grazing dates, fertiliser and irrigation.

Herd software

Most farms use herd management software. Enter events on the same day. Check the daily action lists the software produces, such as cows due for pregnancy diagnosis, cows to dry off and cows still under withdrawal. Back up data regularly.

Checking the milk statement

Each month, compare the buyer's statement with your own records:

  1. Add up your collection slips and compare total litres.
  2. Check the price per litre and any quality bonuses or penalties for bacteria, SCC, fat and protein.
  3. Check deductions such as transport or levies.
  4. Report differences to the manager so they can be queried.

Example: your slips add up to 182 400 litres but the statement shows 180 900 litres. The difference of 1 500 litres at R7.20 per litre is R10 800, worth querying.

lessons.title: People, stores and purchasing
lessons.html:
Staff administration

Supervisors usually provide information that the office uses for wages and HR.

  • Time records: clock cards or time sheets showing hours, overtime, Sunday and public holiday work.
  • Leave: annual, sick and family responsibility leave requests and approvals, in line with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.
  • Training records: who has been trained in what, with dates, such as tractor driving, chemical handling and first aid.
  • Incident register: injuries and near misses as the OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the farm to record and report.
  • Disciplinary records: kept confidential.

Personal information must be handled confidentially in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act. Do not leave staff files open on the desk.

Stores control

A dairy uses many consumables: teat dip, detergents, filter socks, liners, medicines, calf milk replacer, ear tags, fuel. Good stock control prevents running out and theft.

  1. Keep a stock card for each item: received, issued, balance.
  2. Set a minimum level that triggers an order.
  3. Issue stock only against a signature.
  4. Do a physical count monthly and compare with the cards.
  5. Keep medicines locked, with a register for scheduled medicines.

Ordering and receiving

  • Follow the farm's purchasing procedure: requisition, approval, order.
  • When goods arrive, check them against the order and delivery note for quantity, condition and expiry dates.
  • Sign the delivery note, note any shortages and send it to the office.
  • Keep invoices and delivery notes for the accounts.

Check stock cards against a physical count at the end of each month. Large differences can point to recording errors, waste or theft, and should be reported to the manager so the cause can be found and corrected.

lessons.title: Compliance documents and filing
lessons.html:
Documents the farm must be able to show

Milk buyers, auditors, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Employment and Labour, and the local authority may ask to see records. Typical documents include:

AreaExamples
Milk and food safetyMilk buyer contract, quality results, cleaning and temperature records, dairy certificate where required
Animal healthTreatment register, vet visit reports, vaccination and test records, animal movement records
EnvironmentWater use and waste water authorisations under the National Water Act 36 of 1998
SafetyRisk assessments, incident register, training, equipment inspection
LabourEmployment contracts, time and wage records, leave

A good filing system

  • One file or folder per subject, clearly labelled.
  • Newest documents in front, or dated electronic folders.
  • Keep records for the period required by law, buyers and auditors.
  • Scan important paper records and back up electronic files off the computer.
  • Lock away confidential files.

Using admin to improve the farm

Records are not just for inspectors. Monthly, help the manager look at trends: litres per cow, SCC, calf deaths, feed cost per litre, stock usage, overtime hours. Highlight what is getting worse and suggest causes.

Communicating in writing

Write short, clear notes and emails: what happened, when, what you did, what you need. Example: "Tank 2 temperature 9 °C at 06:00, compressor tripped. Reset at 06:10, 4 °C by 07:00. Technician to check today." This gives the manager the facts quickly.

Key points

  • Enter herd and production events on the same day.
  • Check the monthly milk statement against your collection slips.
  • Control stores with stock cards, minimum levels and monthly counts.
  • Keep staff information confidential.
  • File compliance documents so they can be found quickly and back them up.
